title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
content: A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country. The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch. "The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby. Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days. There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury. The AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand. However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade. "He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying. When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified. "Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media. A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened". The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said. Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school. "At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media. "Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred." The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on. "In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment." According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country. High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands. More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according to AFP, with around 85% of them minors. The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike. Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected. Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted. But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets. Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest. In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced. Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October. Calling of a snap election was not a knee-jerk reaction from Pedro Sánchez but a carefully thought-out manoeuvre, Guy Hedgecoe reports from Madrid. Sánchez says Spain will head to the polls on 29 November after recent defeats on measures aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis. A series of measures to tackle the housing crisis were defeated in parliament on Friday Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says the situation in Catalonia remains "very complicated". title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
content: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there. "Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC. "Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?" Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments. "I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC. Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops. US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties. Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges. Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City. The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha. Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough. "I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously." "I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said. Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough." Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island. The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime. The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there. In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government. Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes. In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store. In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman. "Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC. "We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace." Police in Baltimore have said the young girl was not a target of the shooting but was caught in the crossfire. The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions. US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week. It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia, Rubio says
content: The US says it is closely monitoring the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was concern the incident could have led to the spread of pneumonic plague, but that there was no cause for alarm. Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said that "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples". Unconfirmed reports had suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague is found naturally among wild rodents. No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since her death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead. Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution. Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature. "If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that." The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia. The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis , which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death , is found among rodents such as marmots in the area. It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East was founded just over 100 years ago. Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics. "Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said. He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here." "People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said. "It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it." Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible. "Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said. A study suggests London's elite used death toll data to alter their behaviour to navigate the deadly plague. The newborns died during the long New Year holiday in a Siberian hospital. Plaque on the teenager's teeth contains pathogens of the bacteria for the Bubonic plague. The woman, aged about 50, was buried in a Siberian ice cave and discovered millennia later. This was the first recorded death from the disease in Coconino County since 2007. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.
